I gather that my hon. friend said that the statement I made was false. Let me read what the Prime Minister said. I am quoting his words from page 358 of Hansard of November 30 as follows:
We have taken the stand that we shall not subsidize in this connection because to do so would simply mean that any time there is a dispute across this country with a national company involved which affected the public interest so greatly that a stoppage would paralyse Canada it would be known in advance that we would give a subsidy in order to prevent the Canadian economy being paralysed. We do not intend to follow that course.
This statement relates to a subsidy. If you merely replace the word "subsidy" by the word "dispute", we have the same sort of picture. The Prime Minister might just as well have said that any time there is a dispute across this country, with a national company involved, such as the Canadian Pacific Railway or Canadian National Railways and which affected the public interest

so greatly-as the railways do-that a stoppage would paralyse Canada, it would be known in advance that the government and parliament would step in and force them back to work by legislation. It is precisely the same set of circumstances entirely. The Prime Minister admits or says on the one hand that the subsidy would merely entice a need by national companies of this sort- and he can only be referring to the C.P.R. and the C.N.R.-that a subsidy at that stage would entice some sort of need or desire in the future. When he says that he surely must agree that parliamentary action at this time will entice the same sort of desire for parliamentary action in the future and to that extent I say that effectively this freedom to negotiate has been destroyed.
For the second time in 10 years it has been ratified, I should say. It was destroyed in 1950 and this action is a reaffirmation or ratification of the previous action. Future governments and future parliaments will be inclined to take the same action because surely it will not be any less of a national emergency in May of next year than it is now. In this regard perhaps the Minister of Labour would be well advised to take his own advice, namely "Do it now, do not wait for spring", which is the slogan of his department instead of reversing it and saying, "Don't do it now; wait until spring before you do it".
The Prime Minister made another interesting comment to which I should like to refer and as to which I think we need some explanation. Perhaps this should be reflected in the legislation but that is not the situation. The reference is to be found at page 359 of Hansard. The Prime Minister has perhaps already negotiated a collective agreement; I do not know what the situation is. However, near the bottom of page 359 he is reported as having said this:
If there is an agreement to raise wages it shall go back to January 1, 1960.
The Prime Minister knows that statement just is not factual, that if a collective agreement is signed then the terms of the agreement will be what is mutually decided upon between the unions and management. If the Prime Minister is saying that the intent of this legislation is to say that if the collective agreement contains a provision to raise wages it shall be effective as of January 1, 1960, then the legislation should say so. I think perhaps the legislation is deficient in this regard. However, that flat, definite statement is made. The Prime Minister does not qualify it as he usually does by other things; he merely says:
If there is an agreement to raise wages it shall go back to January 1, 1960.

I think that provision should perhaps be contained in the legislation if that is the desire of the Prime Minister and his government. In recent years we have seen a terrific hate labour campaign and in the past three, four or five years it has been intensified. Many people have engaged in it; newspapers with particular axes to grind, organizations with, again, particular axes to grind have engaged in this sort of detestation of labour and have made accusations that it causes all sorts of things.
That hate labour campaign, so-called, has infected a number of people of this country who otherwise should know better but who in many cases do not take it upon themselves to study the question carefully and who are influenced by the inundation of propaganda that has come at them day after day after day for the past four or five years.
To an extent this legislation reflects that sort of inculcation of ideas. It is introduced in that atmosphere that has been developed and which has affected all of us. It has affected and influenced even those people in the trade union movement, those responsible people about whom the Prime Minister spoke. It has affected them to the extent that they say, "I wonder just what, if anything, is wrong within my organization", and they begin to search to find out whether there are not some failings in their particular organizations. In those instances it has a beneficial influence. But it has influenced us all; it has infected us all with this idea. Because it has done this, this legislation partially reflects that attitude.
This is also a question of fundamental rights and human freedoms. Last session- this year, in fact-we had a great debate and discussion in this house. A special committee was established which was a culmination of the Prime Minister's goal, as he said, of many years of endeavour to introduce into Canadian law a bill of rights. We established a bill of rights and it is on the statute books. What does it say? I say that this particular legislation before us is contrary to the bill of rights; it violates it in this instance.
Let me read it to you. This is from the Statutes of Canada 1960, chapter 44, part 1. I will read section 1:
It is hereby recognized and declared that in Canada there have existed and shall continue to exist without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex, the following human rights and fundamental freedoms, namely,-
Then there follows subsection (a), and then:
(b) the right of the individual to equality before the law and the protection of the law;

Maintenance of Railway Operation Act
Do you know, Mr. Speaker, what this piece of legislation that is now before us does? It recognizes the right of the individual to equality before the law, but says that some are less equal than others. There are 110,000 employees in the railway industry in Canada who by virtue of this bill are not going to be equal before the law compared with a number of other workers in this country. They are going to be different. They are going to be denied the right to participate fully under the provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, which is a federal statute. They are going to be denied the right of equality before the law compared with other workers who have that right. That is a violation of the bill of rights and it is completely contrary to the principle of equality before the law. Where is the equality? There is an equality which these 110,000 employees have. Certainly they are equally discriminated against. That is the provision.
This is the result of double meaning in policy statements, thinking in double terms, thinking in terms of political advantage, thinking in terms of what type of legislation may garner a few pieces of support over here but will not help anybody over there. It is the type of legislation that splits and divides, that takes account of splitting and dividing. Perhaps we should have an Orwellian department of double talk or double speak in this government to put this sort of thing into effect.
I am not going to get into the argument of the conciliation board report or the statistical analysis behind it and a comparison of figures. That has been done many tunes.
This is primarily a question of rights. I think parliament should carefully consider what we are being asked to do here, because we are being asked to interfere with the rights of two types of organizations within this nation. We are being asked to interfere with the rights established by law, the right of freedom of association, of freedom to bargain collectively, of freedom to use the full extent of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, of freedom to withdraw from work if workmen so desire-if they see the necessity for it-of freedom to sign collective agreements containing the terms and the provisions that the two parties desire.
What we find has been guaranteed by one law for 20 years is now being repealed; it is being repealed by another law. I for one do not intend to vote for it. I would say also that even though the newspapers have said today, reporting about hon. members in this house-that they would consciously not deliberately debate this bill past the deadline,


so far as I am concerned, if it requires debating and we go past that deadline, I am quite prepared to debate it. I am prepared to debate it whether or not we pass the deadline, if debate is required.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take just a few minutes time in order to make some comment on this most serious matter which is before the house at this time. Without doubt it is a most serious problem and a most serious situation which must have the attention of all hon. members at this time.
I think it goes without fear of contradiction that there is no one in this house who wants to see a tie-up in transportation. It also goes without fear of contradiction that the workers on the railroad who are directly and indirectly affected, and the people of Canada, do not want to see a transportation tie-up, because of course it would be of a very serious nature and everyone admits that it would have a serious impact on the Canadian economy.
It is because of that seriousness that we have to consider the situation as it is at the present time. Mr. Speaker, the first thing that comes to my mind in considering the problems that are facing the unions, the transportation industry and this house is that it gives ample and clear evidence as to what has been stated time after time in the past. It is evidence of the absolute necessity and of the fact that the time has long passed when Canada should have a national transportation policy; that is, an over-all national transportation policy that takes into account the vital importance of transportation, that takes into account all segments of transportation; that is, the railroads in passenger and freight, the airways in passenger and freight, and road transport in buses and in freight.
There is without doubt-and the fact that it was necessary for us to have this debate this afternoon and this evening is clear evidence of this-a vital necessity for working out a transportation policy that recognizes the need of the economy as far as transportation is concerned. There is a vital necessity for a policy that works out plans and directives that will ensure equitable treatment, efficiency as related between the railroad, the airways, the truckers, and guarantees in that policy efficiency of transportation operations, continuity of transportation operation and a guarantee of a proper, decent and reasonable standard of living for all employees in the transportation industry in accordance with their skills and in accordance with the public service that is rendered to the Canadian economy and the Canadian people.

To me that is the most important lesson that we can learn from the situation in which we find ourselves at this time. However, there are one or two items on which I did desire to speak, and I can assure you that I am not going to be repetitive; I am not going to repeat the many arguments, suggestions and analyses that have been put forward by previous speakers.
However, there were several matters upon which I felt impelled to comment at this time. I wish to refer to a statement which the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaber) has often repeated. As I listened to the right hon. gentleman yesterday and today I could not help but note his reference on more than one occasion to the establishment of a standard as regards the remuneration and working conditions of the employees. Having listened to the Prime Minister-and I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that if I was not in my seat I was behind the curtain-I am very sorry to come to the conclusion that ;he question of standards as outlined by him is just as empty in language as, I gather, were the proposals of the railway companies themselves.
I believe, if my memory is correct, that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) speaking of this matter outlined his view of a standard as parity with good employers in outside industry. I think that is a good standard and one which undoubtedly will be acceptable to railroad workers. It has been established for some time that the standard should have reference to the remuneration of employees in the durable goods industry. From my reading of the statements of Mr. Hall and of the union I am led to believe that they would be agreeable to that standard. What they are asking for is that the gap between what they are receiving and the standard in the durable goods industry should be closed. That is the basis of their proposals; that it should not only be closed in the year 1960 but that having been closed it should not be allowed to develop in the future. I believe from what I have read that this would be acceptable to the unions involved and that this is the basis upon which they are asking for justice and equity at the present time.
Having said that, I must turn to what the Prime Minister had to say this afternoon. It certainly was my impression that he was, though perhaps not deliberately, creating the impression that the railway companies had been susceptible to his appeal and the appeal of his colleagues inasmuch as they at least had come forward with some compromise proposal. That compromise proposal as outlined by the Prime Minister was, of course, that suggested by Mr. Gordon of the C.N.R.
Maintenance of Railway Operation Act The right hon. gentleman seemed to give the impression that here the railway companies were trying to come forward with something which would meet the situation, while the union committee was adamant. I do not think that is at all fair. What is the compromise which was suggested by Mr. Gordon? It is definitely my understanding that his suggestion meant that the railways were prepared to come up from a position of zero to approximately two cents an hour in 1960. I do not think we should forget that the compromise which the unions have proposed all along has been one of coming down from their demand for 25 cents an hour to an aceptance of 14 cents an hour as recommended by the Milvain report, and they agreed to this because of their recognition of the importance of the transport industry and the importance of a continuation of service in the public interest. I think we have to consider this and give credit for it to the unions themselves.
I think I should also comment on what might be termed, for want of another phrase, the Gordon offer. As I read the reports and listened to speakers on the government side there would appear to be an indication that the Gordon offer was in the spirit of the Mil-vain proposals. This is not correct at all, because the Milvain award was based on the status quo of government control and regulation as it is exercised at the pesent time and as it will be exercised, now, for a further period of six months. The Milvain proposal is based on the recognition of a standard tied to that of the durable goods industry and trying to close the gap between the two, or at least making a start. That is very clear from the award and from the hearings which were held by the board under Mr. Justice Milvain. On that basis, the basis of starting to close the gap in the 1960 period, the award of the Milvain board for 1960 was seven cents. Therefore the proposal put forward by Mr. Gordon is in no way in the spirit of the Milvain proposal, and there certainly can be no comparison between his compromise offer of two cents and the seven cents laid down in the Milvain award.
I think we have to take note of these things, analyse them in their correct sphere and give credit where credit is due. In this most difficult and serious situation I believe all credit is due to the trade unions, bearing in mind all the time they have spent in negotiation, the voluminous documents and briefs which have been submitted, the answers they have given to all the questions put to them and their willingness to agree to a reduction of their demands from 25 cents to 14 cents in the public interest, as employees in a public service, in order to

Division
accept the award. They have continued to negotiate, but they now find themselves in a position where under the law they must lose that to which they are entitled.
I know that the government and everybody in this house is in a difficult position. Nobody wants a strike. We all want to see justice done, and no matter what we do we are going to be damned-damned if we do, and damned if we don't. It is one of the things in public life which we have to face. I wanted to say these things, and to bring to the attention of the house the need for a national transportation policy based on equity and consultation. I wished also to show in my analysis where I thought the Prime Minister was not being perhaps quite as fair in his statements as he might have been and to endeavour in my own way to present the true picture as I see it.
As I say, we are damned if we do and damned if we don't, but in the light of all the circumstances, considering what has been said and giving due weight to all the principles involved, we have to put it in perspective and I say, on balance, I do not feel I can support this bill in its present form although I know the intention is to avert a strike. I feel this could have been handled in a different way and not left until now, just a few horns before the deadline. Surely reasonable people could have been able to arrive at a reasonable answer so that parliament would not have to face this tough problem.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that if you have made a mistake there is little good niggling away from it. In my remarks of yesterday, according to Hansard, I apparently said, referring to the

people who want a strike, that the only ones I had heard advocate a strike seemed to be the Toronto Globe and Mail, the Canadian trucking association and Mr. Crump. I think I can explain, and I think it is in order that I should. I assumed the Canadian trucking association were prepared for a strike and approved this one coming on because I heard their secretary, Mr. Magee, give a radio talk on CFRA. The whole theme of his radio talk was that if there was a strike the Canadian trucking association was ready to step in and there would not be nearly the dislocation people thought there might be. He used 1950 as a precedent. From that general theme I assumed the Canadian trucking association felt the strike should go on. Apparently 1 was wrong. If I have caused any embarrassment to the Canadian trucking association, I am sorry.
There are, however, other points upon which I should like to touch that have been raised in this debate, particularly by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). In his remarks regarding the negotiations that took place, as I took down his words, he said that the offer of Mr. Gordon had been put to Mr. Hall and Mr. Hall had said it would not be considered. I feel that the Prime Minister should elaborate on that before we continue the debate. He should place on the record what the Canadian National offer was and what was involved. As I understood it, and perhaps he could clear this up, the rejection was not as bald or outright. It was a rejection that was made in the light of the fact the union was very much aware of the details of the Canadian National offer.
As I understood the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), who referred to this, Mr. Gordon related his offer to the durable goods standard referred to in the Mil-vain report, and related it to the average annual increase that has taken place since the first of this year. The point that was obvious to the unions was that if you took the first nine or ten months of either 1958 or 1959 and took the index of durable goods the increase averaged out at about six tenths cents a month. In 1958 and 1959, and in previous years, there was always a spurt of from four to five cents in the last few months in the year. In 1958 and in 1959 the average for each year was seven cents, and for the two-year period it was 14 cents. I imagine that the reason for this concave curve rise is that in the durable goods industry most of their wage contracts are negotiated rather late in the year. I have looked at the dominion bureau of statistics figures myself and there is this striking concave curve which gives you the
Maintenance of Railway Operation Act peak increase late in the year. In the early months there is very little increase.
As a consequence, the Gordon offer based on 10 months would have meant, as I understand it, if you use as comparative examples; 1958 and 1959, for 1958 about 1.7 cents and for 1959 something like 2.5 cents. This is very small and very much below the recommendation of the conciliation board. I think the Prime Minister should fill us in on the details, as he understood them or as his negotiators understood them in connection with this Canadian National offer because I think he has definitely left the impression that the unions, as the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) said, were completely adamant and that they would not even consider the offer. I do not know whether they were prepared to consider it seriously, but they certainly knew what was involved and knew it meant nothing for them that came close to what the majority report of the conciliation board offered.
One other point that the Prime Minister brought up yesterday that intrigued me very much was his suggestion that the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines is going to go into certain issues that have bothered railroaders for some time. He mentioned two things, pensions and turnaround benefits. These two issues have no common link with each other. If such a procedure were adopted, it would certainly take this particular committee into a field in which it has not been operating for a long time. I think it is proper to say here that if we are going to do this, some consideration should be given to what is involved. If turnaround benefits are involved, it means we are going to deal with something which Mr. Gordon and Mr. Crump have said is none of the business of politicians, that is we are going to go into the actual collective agreements that exist between management and labour.
In so far as pensions are concerned, they are considerably different. I think since the Prime Minister raised the issue we should perhaps have further elaboration of it in this very debate. Certainly I would take the Prime Minister's remarks as being, I will not say a sponge tossed out to the railway workers because that is unfair, but certainly a favourable consideration from the government point of view that has been put into this whole discussion.
The last point I wanted to touch upon, Mr. Speaker, relates to a point I brought up and which perhaps needs some elaboration, that is this whole question of some kind of guerrilla warfare that is possible in the next six months on both sides. I received a letter

Maintenance of Railway Operation Act today from a relative of mine who is prominent in union affairs, and the whole theme of that letter was that the railway labour movement is getting rather tired of statesmen as leaders. They are looking for militancy. This bill puts the union leadership in a very difficult position. I should like to emphasize that the whole position of the leaders has been put in jeopardy as a result of this freeze.
Now the obvious retort to this argument is that this must mean the union members are irresponsible. I do not believe it means that at all. It means they are dissatisfied with much more than this particular issue, that they are in a state of insecurity and they are looking for strong leadership. When their leadership is pinched back for a period of six months they can only assume that their leaders have not done a job for them. This gives encouragement to the kind of jurisdictional raids we are quite likely to have. I thought that point might be emphasized, Mr. Speaker.
I can conclude by reiterating that after the kind of debate and discussion we have had this does not look like any better bill than before we had the arguments of the government.

Mr. Speaker, in rising at this time to close the debate on second reading I do so with the deep personal conviction that this measure with which parliament is dealing at this moment is the best possible way to deal with the present situation. I say in all earnestness that this bill is not a measure which, in any way, is designed to undermine the collective bargaining procedure in this country; that, Mr. Speaker, is not the purpose of this bill.
I want to reiterate what I said at the opening of this debate. The purpose of this bill is to extend the present agreements to May 15 and to give the opportunity for collective bargaining any time between now and May 15 in order to arrive at a solution by both parties.
It has been said that on two previous occasions, namely in 1950 and 1958, there were provisions whereby the men were ordered to go back with an increase in pay. I want to point out that we are aware of those cases, of course. In both of those cases, in 1950 and 1958, there was agreement between the parties in the dispute to those arrangements.

The increase in 1958 was as a result of an agreement that had been signed and agreed to by a majority of the employees. On that basis the men were returned to work in 1958.
But implementation of the majority report of the conciliation board at this time, as has been suggested-and I submit this conclusion to the intelligence of the reasonable members of this house-could only be done by compulsory arbitration, and I submit that this procedure would not be acceptable to the labour organizations of this country. I again point out that between 1955 and 1960 out of 79 conciliation boards that were set up, 43 of them brought in reports, 23 of which were rejected by unions and 20 by management. Surely in those 23, if the same procedure had been followed-I realize, as I am sure do all hon. members of this house-that labour would not have acceded to compulsory arbitration or to having the majority reports of the conciliation board imposed upon them by compulsion.
I think it is time, Mr. Speaker, that we got back to what we are actually dealing with. We are dealing with a bill which will do two things. First of all, it will prevent a nation-wide railroad strike with all the effects attendant upon such a calamity. In the second place, it does so without resorting to compulsory arbitration.
This afternoon the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Argue) said the government made up its mind that this national emergency could not take place. He was quite right. Apparently he has not been able to make up his own mind. The same confusion prevails in the ranks of the official opposition. I refer, of course, to labour.
When one examines in some detail this bill and some of the terms that were set out as fundamentals and basic commencements for labour in the bill of 1950, one finds such striking things as these that are absent in this bill:
Provision will be made for provisional terms and conditions of employment of employees and for the final settlement thereof.

I am referring to the preamble of the bill of 1950, where it is said in the fourth paragraph that provision will be made for provisional terms. Here there are no provisional terms whatsoever.
In his summing up on second reading the Minister of Labour seemed to want the house to forget some of the important achievements that were provisional settlements included in the bill of 1950. He referred with some contempt to a guarantee of at least four cents an hour. The reminder apparently was to allow us to forget that one very important milestone incorporated in that bill in 1950 was the establishment of the 40-hour week.
The Minister of Labour indicated also that there was nothing in that bill that had not had the full agreement of both parties to the industrial dispute. That again, I deny and remind the Minister of Labour that that bill brought forward the institution of the 40-hour week earlier than had been agreed upon by the two parties.
I point out that that bill established as a fundamental right of one side of the bargaining unit in addition that their colleagues in the hotel industry who had stood by them in the negotiations would not be ignored and that, despite a lack of agreement, the hotel employees as well as the others would be guaranteed the four cents an hour. In this bill we find none of those fundamentals whatever.
We find no form of achievement in negotiation that had developed, either by unanimous agreement on the part of the conciliation board, or by offers such as the offer that has been referred to in the debate made by the president of the Canadian National Railways, or the proposal that the Prime Minister referred to that was advanced for the purpose of bringing people together by the Minister of Labour, which apparently was an attempt to suggest that half of the 14 cents might be provided if the parties would agree. We find none of those things as a starting point in connection with the consideration of this bill. This is in striking difference to what developed in 1950.
Reference has been made-and I am not going to repeat it-to some of the comments that were made after the government's intention of 1950 was announced. Statements were made by Mr. Bengough, who was the head of the trades and labour congress, and Mr. Conroy, were dismissed with some contempt by a former friend of those gentlemen, the hon. member for Skeena. The hon. member for Essex East is perfectly correct when he says that those gentlemen were certainly not known as well known Liberals. Perhaps hon. members have forgotten that one gentleman in that group who has not
been quoted here today made some comments that were not along the lines of criticism of the minister of labour with respect to what was in the bill of 1950. I refer to the late Mr. Mosher. It is well known that he was no Liberal supporter. When the intentions of the government of that day were made known and the contents of the bill were disclosed to the public, Mr. Mosher was asked a question, and I believe he was alongside of Mr. Hall in the negotiations at that time. He was asked for his comments and he said this, as quoted in the press on August 30, 1950:
I think we might say that the Prime Minister's explanation and his proposed amendment does indicate that it is the desire of the government to see that we do get a fair deal.
Then, he was asked:
Do you think your men are getting a fair deal?
And Mr. Hall this time replied:
Well, I think things will work out all right.
I suggest to the government that they will get no comments from the representatives of organized labour comparable to those that were quoted after the proposals of the government of 1950 were made known. This time, in fact, they will get nothing but bitterness.
The Minister of Labour made some reference to what he thought would be the advantage that would flow from the freeze between now and May 15. He referred to the fact that he expected this would result in a cooling off period. I suggest we will find when we come to tackle this problem again -as we may have to in May-that rather than a cooling off we will have had a continuous boil, boil, boil, and the boil is evident in the comments of organized labour since the intention to provide nothing in the way of advances for labour at this time was announced by the government here. This, of course, is despite the fact that the Prime Minister, in announcing his election campaign after he assumed leadership of his party, and his proposals for labour, said, as quoted in the Toronto Globe and Mail in a speech at Campbellton, New Brunswick, on May 4, 1957:
I have said the C.N.R. must be the model employer for the reason that the state cannot ask private enterprise that which it is not prepared to grant to its employees in crown companies.
Yet, we find that the gap between the wages paid to the employees of the crown railway company and those doing comparable work in comparable industries elsewhere has been steadily widening. The gap is frozen without any consideration or improvement for another six months. I think this indicates, Mr. Chairman, that there is going to be a

This was not the only unanimous recommendation. There was another recommendation that was unanimous, but that one was adverse to the interests of the men. There were other points involved. Is the minister saying that the only discussion that he had with the companies concerned the matter of wages? If that is the case, undoubtedly this government has been remiss in not taking into account in its deliberations, not only the welfare of the companies but the welfare of the men as well. This is a disclosure tonight which if it had been made earlier in this debate would have caused much greater discussion than is now being provided. We are not going to let this matter pass at this stage if the minister tells us again that at no time did he ask the companies whether they would be prepared to accept the majority award.
I go further. It was not necessary to ask the companies to agree to this unanimous award to have it included. It ought to have been included by the nature of the unanimity itself. The government did not hesitate to impose terms against the Canadian Pacific Steamships Company in 1958 in respect of those workers not covered by agreements between the company and the stewards. I refer to the additional eight cents. If that could have been done then, why could not this unanimous award at least have been included so that, instead of the government now facing the charge that they passed this bill without doing anything whatsoever for labour, they might at any rate have been able to incorporate in the bill a provision that would have provided labour with the

In order that the facts may be before the committee I would draw hon. members' attention to the statement made by the railways to the Canadian Press which appears on page 22 of Hansard of August 29, 1950 and sets out fully what the railways had agreed to.
They had agreed to four cents for the railway employees. They had agreed to two cents an hour for the hotel employees, and they had agreed to the 40-hour week only in the year beginning on September 1, 1951. The terms that were in Mr. St. Laurent's bill were not the same as these. They were considerably more generous. The four cents was applied to all classes of employees engaged in the dispute for the reason that I gave this afternoon, namely that Mr. St. Laurent did not wish, by the action of parliament, to create division between one group of employees and another. This term was imposed on both companies by this parliament and it was not agreed to by the railways. The 40-hour week, as my friend the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has pointed out, was made

Mr. Chairman, what the hon. member for Laurier is obviously saying is this; he is objecting to the fact that the railways cannot pay this increase in wages. To do that there would have to be no freeze on freight rates. That freeze was put on for a very good reason a year ago by the Prime Minister. It was because of the unfairness that had been perpetrated during 22 years of Liberal rule on the western and maritime parts of this country, unfair freight rates which were made more and more unfair every time a horizontal increase was put into effect under the Liberal government. They did not bother about it at all; they thought it was a very good thing; they did not care whether the western and maritime parts of Canada had a good deal; they thought it was grand, as long as their people in the central part of Canada were doing all right. They did not think it was important to have a fair deal for everybody in all ten parts of this country. So they objected to this freight rate freeze that we put on. Therefore this royal commission was appointed to find a way of fairly distributing increases in freight rates across all parts of this country.
That is something this government is doing, and it is something that your government refused to do for 22 years, because you did not care to have a fair deal for people in all parts of the country and you did not do anything about it.

At that time it was considered that this railway would be operating for the benefit of the people in northern Ontario and would be a partial repayment from southern Ontario for the advantages derived from the natural resources and the developments taking place in northern Ontario. This railway, over the years, has operated to some extent as a developmental railway but also has operated as a very successful financial enterprise. While it is true the railway has a liability in the form of a loan for $30 million from the Ontario government, last year they showed a balance of $26 million in their financial statement.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, it would be very difficult to use the arguments in connection with the Ontario Northland railway that have been used in connection with the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways. It would seem to me that in passing this legislation we have taken from these employees the right to continue negotiations with this company. The Ontario Northland railway is probably not in a position to take advantage of the right to make application for increased freight rates to the same extent as the other railways because it is truly a provincially nationalized railway and is operated by the provincial government as a developmental railway.

It is the one which the minister said made provision for new collective agreements to take place or for amended or revised agreements to take place between the parties. In connection with clause 3 I think we should consider this matter, as has been done on previous occasions. If we are going to abrogate the right of people in this country for, to put it graciously, a period of some months, as the Prime Minister said, surely we should think in terms of what some of the provisions in that collective agreement should be. That procedure was adopted on past occasions. It was something that was done in 1950. There was a great deal of dispute about that matter a while ago, as to just how this result came about and whether or not there was actual agreement at that time. It was done in 1958 with the 8 per cent wage rate increase, I believe. From memory I think it was 8 per cent. I refer to the provision for an increase in the wages of the employees by virtue of the statute itself. I think this is the clause under which we should discuss that same sort of thing.
In the so-called Milvain report or the report of the conciliation board there are two or three provisions dealing with wages or various wage rate increases at various times throughout the year and there is one dealing with the question of vacations with pay. I think perhaps we should separate our consideration of the two matters and deal in terms of vacations with pay as a separate item from that of the wage rate increase. The Milvain report or the conciliation board report, in so far as the matter of vacations with pay is concerned, near the bottom of the report, recommended
416	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Maintenance of Railway Operation Act that vacations with pay provisions be altered to provide for four weeks or 20 working days after 25 years of service. That is compared with what I think is now 35 years of service before one can reach that position where he has these vacations with pay.
It would be our thought that there should be attached to clause 3 a subparagraph or subsection which in effect would say that the recommendations of the conciliation board dealing with vacations with pay of four weeks or 20 working days after 25 years' service should be contained as a statutory provision. In fact, I have an amendment drafted to this effect, Mr. Chairman, but perhaps I will refrain from putting it forward in a formal way at the moment and go on to the question of the wage rate structure as recommended by the conciliation board.
From my personal point of view-and I am sure from that of many of the workmen themselves-I might say that in the long run the vacation with pay provision is far more important than is the wage increase.
I say this because vacations with pay are considered to be a sort of non-monetary item in the sense they are not a matter of direct wages and they are usually the most difficult things to negotiate for and in the negotiations they are the easiest things to hold on to in a collective agreement whereas wages are the easiest thing to bargain for and the easiest thing to give away. For these reasons-and I have others-I think that to make provision for extended vacations with pay recognizing long term service of employees is the only decent thing to do. I think perhaps these are extremely important provisions.
As to the recommendation in so far as a new two-year contract is concerned, may I say this. Incidentally, if it were in effect, one year of it would already have almost elapsed because it would have been entered into from January 1, 1960 and it would expire at the end of this year. In any event, the recommendation of the conciliation board is that there be two cents per hour increase in wages effective on the first day of January,
1960 and that there be an additional five cents an hour effective the first day of September, 1960 making at that time a seven-cent an hour increase compared with the present collective agreement and that there also be an additional increase of 4 per cent of wages which existed immediately prior to the first day of January, 1960 and to be effective on the first day of May, 1961.
In so far as the 4 per cent is concerned, it is computed on wages at the end of December of this year and shall become effective or is to become effective, according to

the recommendation, 15 days prior to the actual intended expiry date of this particular piece of legislation before us. In the desire not to trample upon the report of the royal commission which is expected about that same time and allowing the negotiations to be conducted from that time forward, based upon what might be in the royal commission's report, it certainly appears that the government wants to carry through its initial objective in this regard. In order to allow for this result to take place, perhaps we should allow the 4 per cent recommendation not to be contained within the statutory provision.
These employees have been negotiating for almost a year. The conciliation board recommended these amounts of money. It did not at that time, I am sure, expect that the Prime Minister and the government would interfere in matters and protract the period of negotiations into some time next spring.
In any event, I think the least we can do -the very least we can do-in consideration of what we are taking away in terms of rights and freedoms of the individual workman in this industry is to provide by statute -as has been the practice on the past two occasions that this has occurred-that they have four weeks' vacation with pay after 25 years of service, as recommended. Also, we should provide that they be paid two cents per hour effective January 1 this year, and an additional five cents per hour effective September 1 this year, as was recommended by the conciliation board.
I think this would be in keeping with whatever sense of appreciation we have left of the value that these people have in our economy, and would partially atone for that which we are taking away from them and denying them by virtue of this statute.
Therefore, I think we should add an additional clause to the bill, I would accordingly move, Mr. Chairman, that clause 3 be changed to subsection (1) and the following added as subsection (2), which would read:
The terms of each existing collective agreement are provisionally amended forthwith on the commencement of this act by increasing by two cents per hour each rate of wages established by or pursuant to the collective agreement effective from the first day of January, 1960, and by further increasing by an additional five cents per hour each rate of wages established by or pursuant to the collective agreement effective from the first day of September, 1960.

I have here if anyone would like to have it. I am sorry I have not additional copies available.

I think, Mr. Chairman, that this is a separate item and should be considered as a separate item. It is the least we can do for the 110,000 employees whose rights have been abrogated at least for a period.

This government has always said that it was not a government that wants to take needlessly powers by order in council. I would therefore assume that they would not put into a clause dealing with regulations matters which they did not feel it was necessary to put in or matters which refer to regulations that they would not propose to use if necessary. Despite all that has been said about abhorrence by this government of compulsory arbitration I find that when the regulations were last presented by this government in legislation of this nature, as the Minister of Labour calls them, we had in section 7 clause (c) phrases such as these:
7. The governor in council may make regulations ...
(c)	for establishing procedures for effecting a settlement between the company and a union and for concluding a collective agreement in revision or amendment of the existing collective agreement; and
(d)	for referring to a board of three arbitrators appointed by the governor in council such matters relating to the revision or amendment of an existing collective agreement as the parties thereto may request-
That part is voluntary but here is the compulsion:
-or as the governor in council may deem expedient,-
My point is that when we had last had what you might call legislation of a similar nature we had the intentions of the government to an extent spelled out. But I never saw under these circumstances more of a blank cheque than what is asked for here. Here we have brevity but we have extreme wideness of opportunity because it provides that, in the context or for the purposes of this bill, the right to make such regulations as the governor in council deems necessary or desirable for the purposes of carrying out any of the provisions of this act. We are not given any outline of possible intentions, even such as that which was given the last time legislation of a similar nature was presented in 1958 and which had reference to the steamship strike settlement of that year.
